In Ableton Live, a tap point is the place in one track's signal path where another track picks up its audio. To tap a track is to take a copy of its signal from that point, leaving the source track's own sound unchanged.
Set it on the receiving track: Audio From names the source track, and Input Channel picks the tap point (Ableton/Live/UG/17 Routing and IO/05 Internal Routings/01 Internal Routing Points):

How can I turn a mono signal into stereo in a channel in Ableton/Live?

Short answer: the channel is already stereo and carries the same signal twice, so the work is making the left differ from the right. Utility's Width knob will not do it. Reach for a device that puts a different signal on each side: Delay with Stereo Link off and unequal left and right times, Chorus-Ensemble, a reverb, or an Audio Effect Rack holding two chains panned hard apart with a few milliseconds of delay on one of them.

00:00 In this video, we're going to take a look at linked tracks. Using the Link Track feature allows you to adjust multiple tracks to edit or adjust parameters. A great use for this feature is when you've recorded multiple sources at the same time.

00:17 So for example, in this case, I have a multi mic recording of some drums in this project. Linking tracks is a very simple procedure in the arrangement view. All I have to do is select the tracks I'd like to link together,

00:33 right click to access the context menu and select Link Tracks. When tracks have been successfully linked together, there's a small icon indicating linked tracks in the top right-hand corner of each track.

00:46 Now, if I go into my Arrangement View and select any of the clips from the linked tracks, all of the linked tracks are highlighted. With the tracks linked, you can now perform all kinds of edits to all the linked tracks. For example... Splitting and deleting selections.

01:13 Reversing selections. Or adding cross-fades and fades. And even renaming selections. You can also manipulate warp markers and warp parameters of all linked tracks. Another great feature of Linked Tracks is the ability to adjust parameters in the mixer section.

01:56 By selecting one of the tracks in a Link Track selection, you're able to adjust the mixer parameters of that particular track. In this state, you can continue to work on other individual tracks and adjust their mixer parameters.

02:20 If you wish to work on all of the linked tracks at the same time, simply click on the Link Track icon and adjust their parameters. This allows for a great amount of flexibility for you to either adjust individual parameters in the mixer section,

02:37 or adjust them all collectively together. Not only can you link together Audio tracks, but you can also link together MIDI tracks. or a combination of MIDI and Audio tracks. As a final technique, Link Tracks can also be used to comp together
03:04 several takes from several tracks simultaneously.
Hiding complexity behind an interface so that higher-level reasoning can proceed without knowledge of lower-level details.
Abstraction works in layers: each level exposes a simplified model and conceals its implementation beneath it.
1. A function abstracts a sequence of steps.
2. A module abstracts a set of functions.
3. An API abstracts an entire system.
Interface vs. implementation: the caller sees what something does; the abstraction decides how.
Information hiding: irrelevant detail is suppressed, not just renamed.
Composability: abstractions can be stacked — each layer need only understand the one immediately below it.
Abstraction makes Declarative programming possible: to declare what should happen, there must be a layer that handles how.
Imperative code is often the implementation layer that a good abstraction hides.
An abstraction leaks when hidden implementation details escape into the interface — forcing callers to know things the abstraction was supposed to conceal.

Abundance is a condition in which people can obtain enough of the goods, services, infrastructure, and opportunities needed to live and act well. In politics, an abundance agenda asks how institutions can make essential things easier to build and provide.

The word names both a material condition and a political project. A promise of abundance is not evidence that a technology will make every scarce resource plentiful or that its benefits will reach everyone.

Greater productive capacity can make some goods cheaper or more accessible. Housing, energy, health care, transportation, and scientific discovery each depend on distinct technologies, institutions, and constraints.
Lower costs can increase demand. Jevon's Paradox describes cases where improved efficiency makes a resource cheaper to use and total use rises, potentially offsetting some expected savings.

More supply can ease prices in the market where supply expands, but a technology's productivity gains do not automatically reduce every price. Demand, bottlenecks, market power, and distribution shape who benefits.

A local wealth shock can raise bids for a scarce asset such as housing even while another sector experiences falling production costs. Those effects can coexist; neither alone describes the overall price level.

Person/Ezra Klein/Book/25/Abundance by Person/Ezra Klein and Person/Derek Thompson argues for a politics that can build more housing, clean energy, and other public goods, and examines institutions that limit that capacity.
Simon & Schuster's publisher page for Abundance describes the book's argument and identifies both authors.
